subject: pathology
title: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome, Ataxia Telangiectasia, and AIDS Pathogenesis

steps.tx: A boy with eczema from infancy, bleeding from small dysfunctional platelets, and recurrent infections carries a cytoskeletal defect in haematopoietic cells caused by mutation of the WAS gene on the X chromosome. Small platelet size distinguishes this condition, the classic triad defining **Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome**, from other bleeding disorders of childhood.
steps.say: Eczema, bleeding with small platelets, and recurrent infections in a boy spell Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

left.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
points: Low IgM, raised IgA and IgE

right.title: Immune thrombocytopenia
points: Large young platelets, normal count recovery

steps.tx: Begin with the infant in front of you rather than the laboratory report. Crusted eczema covers the skin from early life, while bruising hints at platelets that are both few and unusually small, as the film inset shows. That pairing of eczema with tiny platelets is the bedside face of **Wiskott Aldrich syndrome** before immunoglobulin results return.
steps.say: This infant pairs early eczema with bruising from platelets that are few and small, as the inset film shows. Eczema plus tiny platelets is the bedside face of Wiskott Aldrich syndrome.

vis.caption: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome infant with eczema and a blood film inset showing small platelets. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Progressive cerebellar ataxia appearing in a toddler, followed by oculocutaneous telangiectasia of the conjunctiva and ears, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, and extreme clinical radiosensitivity, reflects failure to repair DNA double strand breaks after ionising radiation and normal metabolic damage. The ATM kinase defect behind it also raises alpha-fetoprotein and lymphoma risk, defining **ataxia-telangiectasia**.
steps.say: Toddler ataxia plus conjunctival telangiectasia and raised alpha-fetoprotein point to ataxia telangiectasia, a DNA repair disorder.

vis.alt: DNA double strand break repair defect
vis.caption: DNA double strand break repair failure, the molecular basis of ataxia telangiectasia and its radiosensitivity.

steps.tx: Human immunodeficiency virus enters CD4 T cells and macrophages through its gp120 envelope protein binding CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4 coreceptors, then integrates proviral DNA using reverse transcriptase and integrase. Preferential loss of gut associated CD4 cells occurs within weeks, beginning the long depletion that ends as **acquired immunodeficiency syndrome**.
steps.say: HIV uses gp120 to bind CD4 and a coreceptor, integrates into the host genome, and depletes gut CD4 cells within weeks.

vis.caption: Diagram of HIV entry, reverse transcription, integration, budding and drug targets. Illustration: StewardMD original. [Alt: CD4 T cell diagram showing HIV attachment, reverse transcription, proviral integration, budding, and boxes naming antiretroviral drugs at each step.]

steps.tx: Without treatment, viral replication and immune activation destroy roughly fifty to one hundred CD4 cells per microlitre each year, while viral load set point predicts the speed of that decline. Opportunistic diseases cluster at predictable thresholds, Pneumocystis below two hundred and CMV or MAC below fifty; the measurement guiding all staging is the **CD4 count**.
steps.say: The CD4 count stages HIV: Pneumocystis appears below two hundred, while CMV and MAC wait until below fifty.

rows: Add MAC prophylaxis if not virally suppressed

steps.tx: Kaposi sarcoma, caused by human herpesvirus 8, produces violaceous plaques and nodules on skin, mouth, gut, and lung in advanced HIV, and can flare paradoxically when immunity recovers after starting therapy. Effective antiretroviral therapy is itself the first treatment, with chemotherapy for visceral disease; the virus driving these lesions is **human herpesvirus 8**.
steps.say: Violaceous plaques in advanced HIV mean Kaposi sarcoma driven by HHV-8; starting effective ART is its first treatment.

vis.caption: Kaposi sarcoma violaceous plaques of skin in advanced HIV infection.

steps.tx: HIV associated lymphomas, including diffuse large B cell, Burkitt, and primary CNS lymphoma, arise at higher rates because failed T cell surveillance releases Epstein-Barr virus driven B cell proliferation. Primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS is almost always EBV positive and typically appears below fifty CD4 cells; the surveillance failure centres on lost **EBV-specific T cell control**.
steps.say: When T cell surveillance fails, EBV driven lymphomas emerge, including primary CNS lymphoma at very low CD4 counts.

left.title: At higher CD4 counts
points: ART reduces but does not erase risk

steps.tx: Modern antiretroviral therapy combining two nucleoside agents with an integrase inhibitor suppresses viral load to undetectable levels, restores CD4 counts, and makes sexual transmission effectively zero. Treatment is offered to every patient regardless of CD4 count, a policy summarised as **universal antiretroviral therapy** with treatment as prevention.
steps.say: Treat everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count; an undetectable viral load means the virus is not sexually transmitted.

steps.tx: Wiskott-Aldrich and ataxia telangiectasia share a warning with HIV care: immune defects declare themselves through pattern recognition, unusual organisms, unusual severity, or autoimmunity and malignancy arriving too early. Splenectomy is avoided in Wiskott-Aldrich where possible because of sepsis risk, and definitive cure needs stem cell transplant; that pattern habit is **immunodeficiency pattern recognition**.
steps.say: Unusual organisms, unusual severity, and early autoimmunity or malignancy should always trigger an immunodeficiency workup.
